question: Who is named with Paul in the letter’s opening greeting?

studyGuide.summary: Paul opens the letter by identifying himself as called to be an apostle and naming Sosthenes as a brother alongside him.

memoryAid.text: Corinth was destroyed by a Roman army and later refounded as a colony by Julius Caesar. The Corinth that received Paul’s letter was a rebuilt Roman city on an older Greek site.

question: What does Paul say the people sanctified in Christ Jesus are called to be?

studyGuide.summary: Paul addresses the church in Corinth as people made holy in Christ and called to holiness, together with believers who call on Jesus elsewhere.

memoryAid.text: The Greek word Paul uses for church is also used in the Greek Old Testament for Israel’s assembly at Horeb. Paul’s greeting brings that older picture of people gathered before God into a Roman city.

question: What reason does Paul give for thanking God for the Corinthians?
options: God gave them grace in Christ Jesus
They had baptized the whole city
answer: God gave them grace in Christ Jesus

studyGuide.summary: Paul’s thanksgiving is directed to God because the Corinthians had received grace in Christ Jesus.

memoryAid.text: Notice what Paul is willing to thank God for before raising difficult concerns. Later he says some of their gatherings do more harm than good. Gratitude and a frank account of a problem can belong to the same letter.

question: Whose household had told Paul about quarrels among the Corinthians?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says people connected with Chloe’s household had informed him that quarrels were occurring among the believers.

memoryAid.text: Paul asked another church to read his letter to everyone. If Corinthians was read in the same way, imagine hearing Chloe’s household named aloud in a room where the people involved in the quarrels could hear it too.

question: Which set contains all four names used in the Corinthians’ competing claims of belonging?

studyGuide.summary: Paul reports four competing claims centered on Paul, Apollos, Cephas, and Christ, then challenges the divisions.

memoryAid.text: Acts describes Apollos as an able teacher and shows Priscilla and Aquila helping him learn. At the end of this letter, Paul says he urged Apollos to visit Corinth. Their cooperation reads very differently from the factions claiming their names.

question: After asking if he was crucified for them, what does Paul ask about their baptism?
options: Were you baptized in the name of Paul?
Who taught you before your baptism?
When did you first hear the gospel?
How many of you were baptized?
answer: Were you baptized in the name of Paul?

studyGuide.summary: Paul’s questions point away from personal factions: he was not the one crucified for them, and their baptism was not into his name.

memoryAid.text: Paul remembers baptizing Crispus, and Acts identifies Crispus as a synagogue ruler whose household believed. Even someone with that public standing received baptism in Christ’s name.

question: What did Christ send Paul to do?
options: Build a following around his own name

studyGuide.summary: Paul contrasts his commission to proclaim the gospel with baptizing in this argument, while warning against rhetoric that would empty the cross of its force.

memoryAid.text: In Acts, Paul’s Corinthian ministry starts alongside a tentmaking job with Aquila and Priscilla. He reasons in the synagogue on Sabbaths and ends up teaching in Corinth for a year and a half.

question: For those who are being saved, what does Paul say the message of the cross displays?

studyGuide.summary: Paul contrasts reactions to the cross: those who are perishing regard its message as foolish, while those being saved know it as God’s power.

memoryAid.text: The verse after Paul’s statement about the cross quotes Isaiah. The original passage pictures a clay pot talking back to its maker, a vivid picture of what happens when human wisdom treats God as the one who needs explaining.

question: How does Paul describe Christ to those who are called?
options: The power of God and the wisdom of God
answer: The power of God and the wisdom of God

studyGuide.summary: Paul says that for the called, from both Jews and Greeks, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom.

memoryAid.text: In a defense speech, Cicero treats even the mention of a cross as beneath the dignity of a Roman citizen. Against that background, Paul’s description of a crucified man as God’s power and wisdom would have sounded startling.

question: Why does Paul say God chose what the world regards as foolish and weak?
options: To put the wise and strong to shame
To make social rank the measure of wisdom
To reward people merely for lacking education
To remove every use of human ability
answer: To put the wise and strong to shame

studyGuide.summary: Paul says God chose what the world regards as foolish and weak in order to shame what the world regards as wise and strong.

memoryAid.text: When Samuel is sent to anoint a king, David is still out tending sheep and has to be called in. The story gives Paul’s pattern of overlooked people a face.

question: What does Paul say no one should do in God’s presence?

studyGuide.summary: Paul moves from the Corinthians’ calling to God’s choice of the lowly and overlooked, concluding that no one can boast before God.

memoryAid.text: In chapter 4, Paul puts himself on the low side of the social ladder. He describes going hungry, getting poorly treated, and working with his hands. The logic of God’s choice reaches the apostle too.

question: According to Paul’s concluding instruction in chapter 1, where should boasting be directed?

studyGuide.summary: Paul ends this part of the argument by directing any boasting away from human status and toward the Lord.

memoryAid.text: Paul’s closing line echoes Jeremiah, who names wisdom, might, and wealth as things people brag about. He then describes knowing a God who practices lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness.

question: What did Paul resolve to keep at the center of his message among the Corinthians?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says he deliberately centered his proclamation among the Corinthians on Jesus Christ crucified.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom imagines a listener expecting Paul to overcome a difficult message with impressive delivery. He sees Paul’s simple proclamation of the cross as an essential part of how its power came through.

question: How does Paul describe his own condition when he was with the Corinthians?

studyGuide.summary: Paul describes his presence among them in terms of weakness, fear, and much trembling rather than self-display.

memoryAid.text: Acts supplies a scene behind Paul’s admission of fear. The Lord tells him in a vision to keep speaking and says He has many people in Corinth. Paul then stays to teach for eighteen months.

question: In what does Paul want the Corinthians’ faith to rest?

studyGuide.summary: Paul connects his manner of preaching with its purpose: their faith should have its foundation in God’s power, not in human wisdom.

memoryAid.text: In his next letter, Paul develops the same idea with a picture of treasure carried in clay jars. The ordinary container makes the source of the power easier to see.

question: When did God ordain the hidden wisdom Paul describes?

studyGuide.summary: Paul contrasts God’s hidden wisdom, planned before the ages for our glory, with the wisdom of this age and its rulers.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom pictures one man trying to prove that he can cross an ocean with no ship and another actually crossing by trusting a ship and its crew. He uses the image to show the limits of confidence in one’s own expertise.

question: Whom did the rulers of this age crucify?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says the rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory and that they would have acted differently if they had known God's wisdom.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom lists philosophers, speakers, and speechwriters among the powerful people he hears Paul describing. That reading helps a modern reader see how public speech itself could confer power in an ancient city.

question: What does the Spirit help believers know?
options: The things God has freely given them
To gain control over the rulers of the age
To replace the need for Christ’s cross
To become known for persuasive speaking
answer: The things God has freely given them

studyGuide.summary: Paul says believers received the Spirit from God so that they could understand what God has freely given them.

memoryAid.text: At the end of this argument, Paul echoes Isaiah’s question about who could teach God. Isaiah has just imagined God measuring the sea in His hand. The scale of that picture makes Paul’s claim that the Spirit brings understanding all the more striking.

question: Who watered after Paul planted?

studyGuide.summary: Paul planted, Apollos watered, and God gave the increase.

memoryAid.text: Acts gives the watering a backstory. Apollos taught in Ephesus, received further instruction from Priscilla and Aquila, and then went to Achaia, the region that included Corinth.

question: Who is the foundation Paul says has already been laid?

studyGuide.summary: Paul identifies Jesus Christ as the one foundation.

memoryAid.text: Ephesians gives the same building image a different angle. There Christ is the cornerstone that holds the structure together, and the whole community grows into a temple.

question: What does Paul call the Corinthians because God’s Spirit dwells in them?

studyGuide.summary: Paul calls the Corinthians God’s temple and says God’s Spirit dwells in them.

memoryAid.text: At the dedication of Solomon’s temple, the glory of God fills the building and the priests cannot enter. Paul applies that old image of God’s presence to a quarrelling congregation.

question: What must a steward be found to be?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says faithfulness is required of stewards.

memoryAid.text: Xenophon uses estate management as an example of a skill someone can practice on property that belongs to someone else. That makes Paul’s image concrete. A steward has real responsibility for goods they do not own.

question: What will the Lord reveal when He comes, besides hidden things in darkness?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says the Lord will reveal the counsels of the hearts.

memoryAid.text: Samuel once saw a likely king in Eliab. God redirected him from appearance to the heart. Paul similarly points to something a human evaluator cannot fully see.

question: Whom did Paul send to remind the Corinthians of his ways in Christ?

studyGuide.summary: Timothy was sent to remind them of Paul’s ways in Christ.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom notices that Timothy is sent to remind the Corinthians of a way of life. Their teacher’s absence puts what they already learned into their own hands.

question: What does a little leaven affect?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says a little leaven leavens the whole lump.

memoryAid.text: Jesus uses leaven to picture hypocrisy. Paul applies the same kitchen image to a congregation’s tolerance of wrongdoing. In both cases, a small beginning can spread.

question: Whom does Paul call our Passover?

studyGuide.summary: Paul calls Christ our Passover and says He was sacrificed for us.

memoryAid.text: Josephus connects the annual Passover sacrifice to Israel’s rescue from slavery in Egypt. That remembered rescue is the background when Paul puts Christ at the center of the feast.

question: Which group does Paul ask the Corinthians to judge?

studyGuide.summary: Paul directs this judgment toward those inside the community.

memoryAid.text: Paul ends the chapter with a line that echoes Israel’s law about removing evil from the community. The echo connects his ruling to a much older practice of holding the community responsible for what it permits.

question: Whom does Paul say believers will judge, in addition to matters of this life?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says believers will judge angels.

memoryAid.text: In Plato’s dialogue Euthyphro, Socrates is shocked to meet a man prosecuting his own father. Paul brings that unsettling idea of taking one’s own people to court into the church and calls the disputants brothers.

question: Of whom does Paul say the believers’ bodies are members?

studyGuide.summary: Paul calls their bodies members of Christ.

memoryAid.text: Later, Paul gives this image a social dimension. A member of Christ’s body has a responsibility to the other members, so the pain of one belongs to the whole body.

question: Whose temple does Paul say the believer’s body is?

studyGuide.summary: Paul calls the body a temple of the Holy Spirit.

memoryAid.text: On the Day of Atonement, the sanctuary itself had to be cleansed because it stood among the people. That older picture adds force to Paul’s claim that what we do with our bodies matters when God’s Spirit dwells in them.

question: What does Paul say God has called believers to when discussing an unbelieving spouse who departs?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says God has called believers to peace.

memoryAid.text: In Romans, Paul adds a practical limit to the duty to live peaceably. One person can take responsibility for their part, and the other person still makes their own choices.

question: What does Paul tell the Corinthians to avoid becoming after being bought at a price?

studyGuide.summary: Paul tells them to avoid becoming slaves of men.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom reads this passage as a claim that even slavery cannot prevent a person from belonging to Christ. Paul has just called a Christian slave the Lord’s freed person. He applies the same claim of belonging to a person who is legally free.

question: Whom does Paul say the unmarried man is concerned with pleasing?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says the unmarried man cares about the things of the Lord and how to please Him.

memoryAid.text: Paul roots this advice in a larger picture of a world whose present form is passing. He also states his purpose in verse 35, which is to help people serve the Lord with fewer distractions.

question: What does Paul say he will stop eating if food makes his brother stumble?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says he will give up meat in that situation.

memoryAid.text: Excavators at Corinth’s sanctuary of Demeter and Kore found rows of small dining rooms. That gives you a picture of why food and worship could overlap in Corinth and why the location of a meal could matter to someone’s conscience.
memoryAid.source: Corinth Excavations, Sanctuary of Demeter and Kore

question: What does Paul say edifies?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says knowledge puffs up and love edifies.

memoryAid.text: Paul gives a concrete example of building someone up. A person who understands idols may still give up a meal if their example would lead another person to act against conscience.

question: Whom does Paul identify as the one God, from whom are all things?

studyGuide.summary: Paul identifies the one God as the Father.

memoryAid.text: Read this beside Israel’s confession in Deuteronomy. Notice how Paul places the one God and the one Lord together in a discussion about meals associated with other gods.

question: What does Paul say the person who tends a flock has a right to drink?

studyGuide.summary: Paul uses a flock’s milk as an example of a worker sharing in the benefit.

memoryAid.text: Paul makes a case for material support using everyday work. Then he describes his own choice to waive that right so it would put no obstacle in the way of the gospel.

question: What does the law of Moses say must be left unmuzzled while it treads out grain?

studyGuide.summary: Paul cites the law about leaving an ox unmuzzled while it treads grain.

memoryAid.text: Josephus gives a memorable reason for the law about the ox. The animal has worked alongside the farmer and deserves a share in the fruit of that work. Paul takes the rule into a conversation about support for people who teach.

question: What does the winning runner receive in Paul’s illustration?
options: A place on the next team

studyGuide.summary: Paul urges his readers to run with the aim of obtaining the prize.

memoryAid.text: The Isthmian Games were held near Corinth. Pausanias describes a victor’s crown made of pine. Knowing what a real prize could look like gives Paul’s reference to a perishable crown an edge.

question: Whom does Paul identify as the spiritual Rock?

studyGuide.summary: Paul identifies the spiritual Rock with Christ.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom asks why water came from rock in the wilderness. His answer is that Christ was already present to sustain the people on their journey. That is how he reads Paul’s identification of the rock.

question: What does Paul say the many become because they share in the one bread?

studyGuide.summary: He says the many are one bread and one body.

memoryAid.text: Paul returns to the shared meal soon afterward. Some are hungry while others have plenty, a practical contradiction of the unity that sharing one bread expresses.

question: What purpose does Paul give for eating, drinking, and whatever else believers do?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says to do all such things to God’s glory.

memoryAid.text: The instruction comes after practical advice about buying food and visiting a neighbor for dinner. A grocery purchase or a shared meal is where Paul expects the principle to take shape.

question: Whom does Paul say he imitates?

studyGuide.summary: Paul asks them to imitate him as he imitates Christ.

memoryAid.text: Read the chapter break as a continuous sentence of thought. The example Paul wants copied includes seeking what benefits other people so they might be saved.

question: What does eating this bread and drinking this cup proclaim until the Lord comes?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says the bread and cup proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.

memoryAid.text: Compare Luke’s supper account with Paul’s. Both put the cup after supper and connect it to a new covenant. Paul adds what the gathered church does with that memory. Its meal proclaims Christ’s death until His return.

question: When the Corinthians gather to eat, what does Paul tell them to do for one another?
options: Give one another seats by rank

studyGuide.summary: Paul tells them to wait for one another when they come together to eat.

memoryAid.text: The Greek word Paul uses for supper, deipnon, was an ordinary word for a meal. That makes his rebuke easier to picture. Some people are eating their own suppers, while the gathering is supposed to be the Lord’s supper.

question: For whose benefit is the manifestation of the Spirit given?
options: Only the person who receives it

studyGuide.summary: Paul says the manifestation is given for the profit of all.

memoryAid.text: Paul’s list of gifts includes a little word for practical help. Chrysostom reads it as supporting weak people and puts it among the gifts for which we need God’s help. It gives quiet service a place beside the more visible gifts.

question: By what does Paul say all believers were baptized into one body?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says that all were baptized into one body by one Spirit.

memoryAid.text: In both letters Paul names social boundaries, including slave and free. Galatians adds that those who belong to Christ share in Abraham’s promise.

question: What do all the members do when one member suffers?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says every member suffers with the one that suffers.

memoryAid.text: Just before this, Paul says parts that seem weaker are necessary and deserve honor. Sharing pain belongs to a community where overlooked people already matter.

question: What is missing when impressive speech is compared to noise?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says impressive speech is empty without love.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom explains that even impressive speech falls flat when it does not serve someone in love.
memoryAid.sourceClaim: Chrysostom describes speech without love as sound that serves no good purpose.

question: What does Paul picture extraordinary faith being able to move?

studyGuide.summary: Paul pictures faith strong enough to move mountains. Even faith that powerful needs love.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom connects the image to Jesus’ teaching about faith in Matthew 17:20. The size of the mountain makes Paul’s point vivid. Even great faith needs love.
memoryAid.sourceClaim: Chrysostom connects Paul’s mountain image to Matthew 17:20 and explains why Paul chooses such an astonishing example.

question: What is missing when giving all your goods to feed the poor profits you nothing?

studyGuide.summary: Paul imagines giving away everything to help the poor and asks what such generosity is worth without love.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom notices how far Paul takes the example. The giver gives everything and takes care in distributing it. The example asks us to consider whether we truly care for the people we help.
memoryAid.sourceClaim: Chrysostom emphasizes both the amount given and the care taken in distributing it, even in Paul’s example of giving without love.

question: How does Paul first describe love?

studyGuide.summary: Paul begins his description of love with patience and kindness.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom sees the two qualities working together. Patience holds back anger, and kindness actively helps calm the person who is upset.
memoryAid.sourceClaim: Chrysostom explains that patience can withstand provocation and that kindness goes further by helping calm another person’s anger.

question: Whose interests does love avoid seeking first?

studyGuide.summary: Paul describes love as looking beyond its own interests.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom connects this verse to Paul’s instruction to seek our neighbor’s good. Helping someone else becomes one way both people grow together.
memoryAid.sourceClaim: Chrysostom links this verse to 1 Corinthians 10:24 and explains that each person’s good is bound up with their neighbor’s.

question: What does love rejoice in, according to Paul?

studyGuide.summary: Paul contrasts celebrating wrongdoing with taking joy in the truth.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom connects this verse to sharing another person’s joy. Love can celebrate the good in someone else’s life as readily as its own.
memoryAid.sourceClaim: Chrysostom connects rejoicing in the truth with Romans 12:15 and taking joy in the good of others.

question: What object does Paul use to show how incomplete our understanding is now?

studyGuide.summary: Paul’s image is a dim reflection in a mirror. It points to the difference between what we know now and what we will see clearly later.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom says the dim reflection is a picture of how partial our knowledge is. Paul’s contrast with seeing face to face points to greater clarity to come.
memoryAid.sourceClaim: Chrysostom explains the dim mirror as a sign of partial knowledge and seeing face to face as an image of greater clarity.

question: Which of faith, hope, and love does Paul call the greatest?

studyGuide.summary: Paul names faith, hope, and love and calls love the greatest of the three.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom ties love’s greatness to how long it lasts. When what we have believed and hoped for comes to pass, love continues and grows.
memoryAid.sourceClaim: Chrysostom says the fulfillment of faith and hope leaves love still present and stronger.

question: Which of these does Paul list alongside edification and exhortation as a result of prophecy?

studyGuide.summary: Paul lists edification, exhortation, and comfort.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom reads this verse as a test of whom a gift benefits. He explains the prominence of tongues at the Church’s beginning through the apostles’ need to travel and speak across languages.

question: What word does Paul say a listener cannot say at the thanksgiving if they do not understand it?

studyGuide.summary: Paul asks how the listener can say Amen without understanding.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom points out that the person listening has a real job to do in common prayer. Their Amen joins them to the thanksgiving. If nobody can understand what is being said, the congregation loses its turn.

question: How does Paul say all things should be done?

studyGuide.summary: The chapter closes by calling for decent and orderly practice.

memoryAid.text: The instructions cover more than one kind of participation. Paul asks those who speak to take turns and has others weigh what the prophets say. Order makes room for listening and discernment.

question: On which day does Paul say Christ rose again?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says Christ was buried and rose again the third day.

memoryAid.text: Paul describes passing on a message he first received. Luke connects the third day to Scripture as well, then links the resurrection to the disciples’ job as witnesses.

question: What word does Paul use for Christ in relation to those who have died?

studyGuide.summary: Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

memoryAid.text: The first sheaf of the harvest was brought to God before people ate from the new crop. Paul’s sequence in verse 23 makes the picture clear. Christ comes first and those who belong to Him follow.

question: What does Paul say about the Corinthians’ labor in the Lord?
options: It matters for a short time

studyGuide.summary: Paul encourages steady work because their labor in the Lord is not in vain.

memoryAid.text: Paul imagines how empty preaching and faith would be if Christ had stayed dead. The closing promise about work answers that earlier thought after celebrating victory over death.

question: On which day does Paul tell each person to set something aside?
answer: The first day of the week
options: The first day of the week
The last day of the week
The first day of the month

studyGuide.summary: Paul asks each person to set something aside on the first day.

memoryAid.text: Two letters show the planning behind the gift. People save ahead of time, and the Corinthians approve delegates to carry it. Generosity here has a schedule and a way to protect trust.

question: Until which feast does Paul say he will stay in Ephesus?

studyGuide.summary: Paul plans to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost.

memoryAid.text: Josephus explains the festival’s name by its timing. Pentecost came after seven weeks, on the fiftieth day, and marked an offering from the new harvest. Paul uses that date to tell Corinth when he plans to leave Ephesus.

question: What does Paul say should shape everything the Corinthians do?

studyGuide.summary: Paul tells them to let everything they do be done with love.

memoryAid.text: The call to love follows commands to be watchful, brave, and strong. Paul then ends with his own love for them, bringing the teaching of chapter 13 into the letter’s farewell.

question: Whom does Paul name alongside himself in the greeting?

studyGuide.summary: Paul opens the letter by naming Timothy as a brother.

memoryAid.text: The greeting has a backstory. Acts names Timothy and Silas arriving from Macedonia during Paul’s earlier stay in Corinth. Timothy already knew the city.

question: Why does God comfort Paul and his companions in their troubles?
options: So they will never face trouble again
So they can depend on their own strength

studyGuide.summary: They receive comfort so they can pass that comfort on to people in trouble.

memoryAid.text: Paul soon describes a danger in Asia so severe that he expected to die. He credits the Corinthians’ prayers with helping him, so the care in this letter runs in both directions.

question: In whom are all the promises of God Yes and Amen?

studyGuide.summary: The verse says all the promises of God in Christ are Yes.

memoryAid.text: The argument about Paul’s reliability starts with travel plans. Corinth sat between two harbors, which Strabo says gave it access toward Asia and Italy. A church in a city built around journeys knew how much could depend on a route.

question: What does Paul say he shed as he wrote out of anguish?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says he wrote with many tears so they would know his love.

memoryAid.text: Later Paul admits a letter made them sad and that he briefly regretted sending it. He is glad the sorrow led to a change of heart. The two passages show how uncertain and personal correction could be.

question: What does Paul tell the Corinthians to do for someone who might be overwhelmed by sorrow?
options: Keep reminding him of the offense

studyGuide.summary: Paul asks the community to forgive and comfort him.

memoryAid.text: Paul says the penalty has done enough. He then treats overwhelming sorrow as a danger and asks the community to reaffirm its love. Restoration takes as much attention as correction.

question: Whom did Paul fail to find when he came to Troas?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says he had no rest in his spirit because he did not find Titus.

memoryAid.text: Right after describing an anxious departure, Paul switches to the image of a triumph. Josephus describes a Roman triumph with trophies and captives paraded before the city. Paul gives the victory to God and puts himself in the procession.

question: Where does Paul say Christ’s letter is written, instead of on tablets of stone?
options: On the walls of the temple

studyGuide.summary: Paul pictures Christ’s letter written on human hearts by God’s Spirit.

memoryAid.text: When Apollos went to Achaia, believers sent a letter asking local disciples to welcome him. Paul starts this chapter by questioning whether he needs that kind of letter. He says the Corinthians themselves are the letter others can read.

question: What does Paul say the Spirit gives?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says that the Spirit gives life.

memoryAid.text: The words new covenant recall Jeremiah’s promise that God would put His law within His people. That helps explain Paul’s move from a visible letter to what the Spirit writes in people.

question: What does Paul say is present where the Spirit of the Lord is?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says there is liberty where the Spirit of the Lord is.

memoryAid.text: Moses takes off his veil when he goes in before the Lord. Paul extends that scene to everyone who turns to the Lord and, with an unveiled face, is being transformed.

question: What did God command to shine out of darkness?

studyGuide.summary: The verse recalls God’s command for light to shine out of darkness.

memoryAid.text: Paul reaches back to the first command of the creation story. When he writes about God shining in human hearts, he uses the birth of light itself to describe seeing God’s glory in Christ.

question: What sort of vessels does Paul say hold the treasure?

studyGuide.summary: Paul puts the treasure in earthen vessels so the power is seen to come from God.

memoryAid.text: Clay was ordinary enough that even the broken pieces had uses. Plutarch describes Athenians scratching names on potsherds when voting to exile a citizen. The material in Paul’s image could be cheap, breakable, and readily at hand.

question: What does Paul say is eternal?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says the things that are unseen are eternal.

memoryAid.text: Paul combines two ways to weigh hardship. Its duration is a moment and its weight is light. He sets both against an enduring weight of glory.

question: What kind of building does Paul say believers have from God if their earthly tent is destroyed?
answer: A house not made with hands
options: A house not made with hands

studyGuide.summary: Paul describes a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom follows Paul’s imagery from a tent and house to putting on clothing. He reads the change as a more lasting way to live bodily, with mortality swallowed up by life.

question: What is anyone who is in Christ, according to Paul?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says that if anyone is in Christ, that person is a new creation.

memoryAid.text: Isaiah pictures a new act of deliverance using water in the wilderness after recalling the way through the sea. Paul’s language about old things passing and new things coming invites a similar look at what God can remake.

question: What role does Paul say he and his coworkers have for Christ?

studyGuide.summary: Paul calls them ambassadors for Christ who appeal for reconciliation with God.

memoryAid.text: In Ephesians the same role appears with a twist. Paul calls himself an ambassador in chains. He asks for courage to speak, even when he has the status of a prisoner.

question: When does Paul say the day of salvation is?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says now is the day of salvation.

memoryAid.text: Isaiah’s words about an acceptable time are followed by a picture of prisoners coming out and people finding food and water. Paul takes that promise of rescue and makes the timing immediate for his readers.

question: What does Paul say the ministers are always doing even while sorrowful?

studyGuide.summary: Paul describes himself and his fellow workers as sorrowful yet always rejoicing.

memoryAid.text: Read this as one of a series of paired descriptions. Paul can be regarded as unknown and still be well known, or look poor while making others rich. Each pair gives a different perspective on the same life.

question: Whose temple does Paul say the believers are?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says believers are the temple of the living God.

memoryAid.text: Paul joins an old promise that God will walk among His people with temple language. Ezekiel gave that promise to a people being restored, so the temple here is closely tied to belonging.

question: Who came and brought Paul comfort?

studyGuide.summary: God comforted Paul and his companions by the coming of Titus.

memoryAid.text: The meeting resolves a story Paul left hanging when he departed Troas. Titus also brings an account of how the Corinthians responded. Paul receives comfort from both a person and the news that person brings.

question: What does godly sorrow produce, according to Paul?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom asks when grief actually repairs the thing that caused it. He distinguishes grieving a loss, which cannot bring it back, from grieving a wrong, which can move a person to change how they live.

question: With what attitude does Titus remember the Corinthians receiving him?

studyGuide.summary: Titus remembers being received with fear and trembling.

memoryAid.text: Fear and trembling can sound like terror to a modern reader. Chrysostom hears the phrase here as honor and respect. He points out that Titus remembers their welcome with affection.

question: What hardship did the Macedonians experience even as they gave generously?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says their deep poverty abounded in generous giving.

memoryAid.text: The Macedonians resemble the widow Jesus notices at the treasury. Both stories ask the reader to pay attention to what a gift costs the giver. Paul adds that the Macedonians actually pleaded for the chance to take part.

question: What does Paul say Jesus became for their sakes, though He was rich?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says Jesus became poor for their sakes, that they might become rich through His poverty.

memoryAid.text: What kind of riches could come from Christ becoming poor? In the middle of a collection appeal, Chrysostom points his listeners to forgiveness and holiness. Those are the treasures he hears in Paul’s words.

question: What did the one who gathered little lack?

studyGuide.summary: Paul quotes Scripture saying the one who gathered little had no lack.

memoryAid.text: Paul borrows the line from the manna story. There, a household’s needs determine its share. Here that becomes a picture of a gift traveling between communities so people have enough.

question: How will someone reap if they sow sparingly?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says that the one who sows sparingly will reap sparingly.

memoryAid.text: Paul’s seed image continues a few verses later with language from Isaiah about seed for the sower and bread for food. Seed in the image is something God provides so that people can go on doing good.

question: How does Paul describe the giver God loves?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says God loves a cheerful giver.

memoryAid.text: Deuteronomy tells a giver to watch their own heart, especially when it would be easy to hold back because the year for releasing debts is near. Paul also pays attention to the will behind the gift.

question: What does the Corinthians’ generosity produce through Paul and his coworkers?
options: A new rule for the churches

studyGuide.summary: Paul says this generosity produces thanksgiving to God.

memoryAid.text: Paul follows the money all the way to its recipients. He imagines them thanking God and praying for the givers, so a gift can start a relationship between people who live far apart.

question: What can the weapons of Paul’s warfare pull down through God’s power?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says the weapons are mighty in God for pulling down strongholds.

memoryAid.text: The next verse identifies targets such as arguments and claims raised against the knowledge of God. Paul takes the language of a siege into the realm of what people think and believe.

question: To whom are thoughts brought into obedience?

studyGuide.summary: Paul describes bringing every thought into captivity to Christ’s obedience.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom asks what kind of captivity can be a benefit. He reads the image as rescue from one kind of bondage into service to Christ, turning the expected outcome of a military capture around.

question: In whom should a person who glories glory?

studyGuide.summary: Paul directs anyone who glories to glory in the Lord.

memoryAid.text: Paul ends very different arguments in the two letters with the same instruction. Jeremiah’s background names three familiar grounds for bragging, wisdom, strength, and wealth, then points to knowing the Lord.

question: To whom does Paul say he has betrothed the Corinthians?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says he has betrothed the community to one husband, Christ.

memoryAid.text: A scene from Genesis gives this image a backstory. Abraham’s servant arranges the marriage and brings Rebekah to meet Isaac. Paul gives himself a similar part in a relationship that belongs to Christ.

question: Whom does Paul name as the person deceived by the serpent?

studyGuide.summary: Paul recalls how the serpent deceived Eve through craftiness.

memoryAid.text: The serpent in Genesis begins with a question about what God said. Paul also pictures a threat arriving through persuasive words, here preaching about another Jesus or a different gospel.

question: In what was Paul lowered through a window in the wall?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says he was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall.

memoryAid.text: Paul could have used a daring getaway to make himself sound like a hero. Chrysostom focuses instead on Paul’s willingness to escape in a basket so he could go on preaching. Sometimes courage looks like letting people get you out of trouble.

question: To which heaven was the man in Christ caught up?

studyGuide.summary: Paul describes the man as caught up to the third heaven.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom reads the man as Paul and hears deliberate restraint in the third-person telling. The speaker knows an extraordinary thing happened and twice admits he cannot explain how it happened.

question: In what does the Lord say His strength is made perfect?

studyGuide.summary: The Lord tells Paul that His strength is made perfect in weakness.

memoryAid.text: Paul asked three times for the thorn to go away. The reply he records reshapes what he can expect from Christ in the presence of a difficulty that persists.

question: For what does Paul say he will gladly spend and be spent?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says he will gladly spend and be spent for their souls.

memoryAid.text: A verse earlier, Paul compares himself to a parent who saves for children. He offers more than his resources here, even wondering whether his greater love will be returned with less love.

question: How many witnesses does Paul say establish a matter?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says a matter is established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.

memoryAid.text: The rule comes from Israel’s law about evidence. The same paragraph calls for judges to investigate false testimony, so the number belongs to a larger concern with fair judgment.

question: By whose power does Christ live after being crucified in weakness?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God.

memoryAid.text: Earlier Paul describes carrying the dying of Jesus in his own body so Jesus’ life can be seen there too. He returns to that same pairing when speaking about Christ’s power among the Corinthians.

question: What does Paul tell the Corinthians to examine themselves to see?
answer: Whether they are in the faith
options: Whether they are in the faith
Whether they give more than Macedonia
Whether they can speak in tongues

studyGuide.summary: Paul tells them to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith.

memoryAid.text: The readers want proof that Christ speaks in Paul. Paul turns their demand into a question about whether they can recognize Christ in their own lives.

question: What does Paul say he prays for the Corinthians to become?

studyGuide.summary: Paul says he prays that they may be made complete.

memoryAid.text: Chrysostom hears Paul’s related instruction in verse 11 as filling in what is missing. Look at verse 10 between the prayer and the instruction. Paul hopes that his authority can be used to build people up.

question: Whose communion does Paul name in the final blessing?

studyGuide.summary: Paul closes with the grace of Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit.

memoryAid.text: The same three-part blessing is heard in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy as the Eucharistic prayer begins. A line that once closed a letter is now spoken to a gathered congregation.
